owner.occupation: Volunteer bookings coordinator at a church hall

world.bio: I'm a retired bookkeeper who now runs the bookings spreadsheet for a church hall in Ashfield, in Sydney's inner west. I'm a volunteer, which in practice means I answer the phone, chase the cheques and worry about the electricity bill more than the sermon. The hall has a council-registered commercial kitchen and a main room that holds ninety.
skills_assets: Bookings spreadsheet with five years of history: who hires the hall, when and for how much
A council-registered commercial kitchen: stainless benches, two ovens, large fridge, dishwasher
Main hall seating ninety, small meeting room, an upright piano
Forty years of bookkeeping: can read a profit and loss statement upside down
Knows every neighbour and half the parish, and who owes whom a favour
Can produce a clean profit and loss statement for the hall in an afternoon

projects.name: Weekday bookings drive
projects.text: The hall sits empty Tuesday to Thursday most weeks. The committee voted that unless weekday bookings cover the rise in electricity and insurance, the Friday food pantry gets cut. I'm trying to find regular hirers.

projects.name: Friday food pantry
projects.text: Runs every Friday morning with eleven volunteers and about seventy households. It's the best thing the church does.

projects.name: Hip recovery
projects.text: Six months post-replacement. Walking without a stick for short distances. Physio twice a week.

projects.name: Insurance renewal review
projects.text: Compared three quotes for public liability. The cheapest requires every hirer to hold their own cover. That puts off exactly the small community groups we want. I'm writing a memo to the committee setting out the options.

notes.text: Committee meeting. The electricity bill is up eighteen per cent and the insurance renewal is up twenty-two. The treasurer asked what we could cut. I said the pantry. There was silence. I said that's why we need hirers, not cuts. They voted, after forty minutes, that if weekday bookings don't cover the rise by December, the pantry stops.

Sat with the spreadsheet for two hours. We have regular hirers on Fridays and weekends: a Korean church, a yoga class, a dance school on Saturdays. Tuesday to Thursday is blank. I highlighted it in yellow. Looks like a prairie.

Hip aching in the cold. Took a paracetamol and sat on the hall's back steps. A young man was carrying a cooler into the kitchen next door, the Korean church's. We said hello. He said 'nice kitchen you've got here'. I said 'it's council-registered'. He said 'what does that mean'. I explained it. He said 'we could use that'.
Grandkids this weekend. The older one asked why the church hall smells like soup. I said because people cook here. She asked who. I said all sorts.
Physio says my hip is healing faster than expected. I may be able to ditch the stick for good by Christmas. I told her I'd bake her a lemon cake. She said no cake, just do the exercises.

A woman called to ask about hiring the kitchen for a cooking class. I told her the kitchen is council-registered, so she could sell what she made. She asked how many people it fits. I said eight comfortably. She said she'd think about it. They always say they'll think about it.
Lawn bowls on Wednesday. Lost by two points to Frank. He said 'you're slipping, Maggie'. I said it's my hip. He said 'that's what they all say'.
The roof gutter on the south side is leaking again. The handyman wants $600. The committee won't approve until next month. I put a bucket under it and wrote 'EMPTY ME' on a sign.

Reading the insurance renewal. The public liability premium is now $3,400 a year, up from $2,800. The excess has doubled. I asked the broker if it can be reduced. He said only if we reduce the number of events. That is the opposite of what we need.
Looked at the spreadsheet again. If we got eight weekday hires at $180 each, that would cover it. If we got four regulars paying $90 a week, that would cover it too. Nobody has called to ask.
Went into the empty hall alone and stood in the middle. Dust in the light. Nobody on a Tuesday. It felt like a held breath.

messages.text:
Alan: Maggie, can you work out what weekday income we need to hold the pantry?
Me: About $11,000 for the year.
Alan: Is that realistic?
Me: It's not impossible.

Daughter: Mum, are you sure about the stairs?
Me: I'm using the rail.
Daughter: Please don't carry the cheque box.
Me: I'm not an invalid.

Joan: We had seventy-four households last Friday.
Me: That's the highest yet.
Joan: Eggs ran out at ten.
Me: I'll ask the Kogarah supplier for another dozen trays.

Frank: My nephew's looking for a space for a cooking class.
Me: Does he need a commercial kitchen?
Frank: He's never said.
Me: Tell him to ring me.

Teacher: Can I change from Thursday evening to Wednesday?
Me: I'll check the diary.
Teacher: Thank you.
Me: Wednesday is fine.

relations.about: Runs the Friday food pantry, never tired
Lawn bowls friend, makes fun of her hip

constraints: The hall is for community use; no alcohol-led events
Insurance requires every hirer to sign the hire agreement
Cannot lift heavy furniture because of the hip
sensitive: She is quietly frightened that if the pantry closes, some of the households will go without
Does not tell her daughter how tight the hall's finances are
